analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling off Northern California's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Natural Resources Committee after being referred to a subcommittee in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently barred oil and gas preleasing, leasing, and related activities on the outer Continental Shelf off the coasts of Mendocino, Humboldt, and Del Norte Counties in California, and would have excluded those waters from the government's mandatory inventory of offshore oil and gas reserves [S2][S3]. It grandfathered rights under any leases already issued [S3]. It was introduced in January 2011, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities and businesses in Mendocino, Humboldt, and Del Norte Counties that depend on fishing, tourism, and an unpolluted coastline would benefit if the bill passed, since new offshore drilling leases could no longer be issued in their waters [S2][S3]. It also served environmental protection broadly by permanently shielding a stretch of the Pacific from new drilling activity [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Northern California coastal communities and environment

how_it_helps.text: It would permanently prohibit oil and gas preleasing, leasing, and related activities in the outer Continental Shelf off Mendocino, Humboldt, and Del Norte Counties, removing any risk that future administrations could open those waters to new drilling.

It would exclude those same areas from the mandatory outer Continental Shelf oil and gas reserve inventory required by the Energy Policy Act of 2005, so the federal government could not treat those waters as a future drilling supply.
Existing leases issued before enactment would keep their rights, limiting disruption to any operations already underway.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to any potential new offshore reserves off Northern California's coast, and the federal government would forgo possible lease revenue from that area [S2][S3]. If those reserves contain significant oil or gas, consumers could theoretically face slightly higher energy costs, though the areas were not known producing fields.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers and federal leasing revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently remove a public resource — potential offshore oil and gas reserves — from development and from the federal reserve inventory, which supporters of drilling argue reduces domestic energy supply and federal leasing revenue, particularly during a period of high energy prices.
It is a geographically narrow, permanent prohibition set by statute, so it forecloses future reassessment of the area's resources or environmental tradeoffs as technology or conditions change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded a small, speculative energy-supply and revenue loss for permanent protection of a specific stretch of coastline from new drilling, with existing leases unaffected. For the coastal communities whose economies rest on fishing, tourism, and water quality, the protection outweighs the cost; from a national energy-supply view, the forgone reserves are modest and their size unknown since the bill also kept them out of the federal inventory.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee in January 2011, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson introduced the Northern California Ocean and Coastal Protection Act on January 12, 2011.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on the day it was introduced.
On January 26, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 112th Congress.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a Democrat, in two years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept open the possibility of future leasing off Northern California's coast, since the waters were never permanently protected. The coastal communities that sought protection gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests; coastal protections never advanced

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban offshore oil and gas leasing off his North Coast district; no further action followed.

for.name: 1 House Democrat cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's sole cosponsor.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (Chairman Doc Hastings, R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat at the subcommittee level for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded; the committee that let it die was controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and drilling companies
industries.note: The bill would have permanently barred new leases off Northern California's coast, foreclosing any future drilling in those waters. Because drilling there risks spills that would damage coastal fisheries and tourism, the industry's interest in opening the area runs against the coastal communities' interest in protection.

industries.industry: Northern California coastal fishing and tourism businesses
industries.note: A permanent ban on new offshore drilling in their waters would protect the clean coastline, fisheries, and beaches their livelihoods depend on. Local economies benefit when spill risk is removed.
